events/1308_inferno/phases/0/transitionT: At the lectern, Boccaccio reads a line Dante wrote about himself in the Convivio.
events/1308_inferno/phases/0/announcemen: “I am a ship with no sail and no rudder, blown by the dry wind of poverty to every port, river mouth and shore.” — Boccaccio: “The sixth year of exile. What you are about to see is a man sinking to the bottom, and then picking up his pen down there.”
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/narrative: Living off other people. Verona, the court of the Scala family — your patron's bread, the last seat at the table.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/instruction: Walk about under the arcade. See what it is like to eat at another man's table.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/0/dial: Signor Alighieri, at tonight's dinner you sit at the last place — down by the door.
No offence. Seats go by rank. And you these days… well.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/1/dial: Everyone here has a use: I make my lord laugh, the cook fills him up, the soldiers keep him safe.
A poet? Ha! A poet is the fruit bowl after dinner — nobody notices if it isn't there.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/2/dial: Alighieri! The brothers are gathering. We join the Ghibellines and fight our way back into Florence!
Your name is still on our roll. If you don't come, you're a traitor.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/3/dial: Sir, don't listen to them. Tell me about Virgil — yesterday we got to Book VI, where Aeneas goes down to the world of the dead…
(The young lord of the Scala house, the only one at court who treats him as a teacher. Years later, the Paradiso will be dedicated to the grown-up Cangrande.)
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/narrative: The White envoy stands under the arcade, waiting for an answer. Fight your way home — is that the road home, or the road to death?
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/question: Fight your way home with the exiled Whites?
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/options/0/t: Go. Fight our way into Florence!
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/options/0/r: 20 July 1304, La Lastra. The army of the exiled Whites falls apart. Bodies everywhere. If you had been there, you would already be dead. — Think again.
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/options/1/r:
Your hatred and their hatred are the same thing.
Rather than walk with fools — I will be a party of one (parte per te stesso).
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/conclusion/: After the disaster at La Lastra in 1304, Dante broke with the exiled Whites for good, and from then on he was a party of one. He had lost his last side — and for the first time he was really free. A man with no party to speak for him can only speak to everyone.
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/sin/did:
In life they took money to see the future for other people: who would win, who would die, which day to send the army out.
Some believed it, some were frauds. Dante is putting them in Hell — and the punishment is his to decide.
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/question: If you were writing this part, what would you turn them into?
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/slots/1/lab: So forever after, they can only
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/parts/2/tex: Stuffed head-down into a crack in the rock
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/parts/3/tex: Turned into a stone statue that can't move
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/parts/6/tex: walk the same road ten thousand times
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/danteVersio:
Their heads are twisted around backwards, their faces looking at their own spines. To go forward they have to walk backwards — because they can never see what is in front of them again.
Their tears run down their backs. (Inferno XX)
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/mirror/sin: Alive: had to see what was ahead
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/mirror/puni: Dead: can only ever see behind
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/rule:
Turn the shape of the sin over, and you have the shape of the punishment.
Dante gave this rule a name: contrapasso.

Once you see the rule, you can work out the other eight circles yourself — which is exactly what comes next.
events/1308_inferno/phases/4/transitionT:
The Inferno is being written canto by canto, and copied from court to court.
Late autumn 1308, a messenger bursts in under the arcade —
events/1308_inferno/phases/4/announcemen:
“Through me you go into the city of grief,
through me you go into pain that never ends,
through me you go among the people who are lost.

You who come in, leave every hope outside.”
events/1308_inferno/phases/4/dufu_reacti:
(head snaps up)
…Maybe there is still hope.
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/question: Which language did Dante decide to write the Divine Comedy in?
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/0: Latin — the proper language of scholars and the Church
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/1: French — the usual language of court literature
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/2: The Italian vernacular — “the language the woman in the bakery can read too”
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/3: Greek — the language of the ancient epics
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/explanation: In De vulgari eloquentia Dante defended his mother tongue, and he wrote the Comedy in the Tuscan vernacular — a decision that lifted the “vernacular” into a language for literature, and the reason he is called the “father of the Italian language.”
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/question: When Dante says he is “a party of one” (parte per te stesso), what does he mean?
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/options/0: He started a new political party
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/options/1: He refused to join the exiled Whites and the Ghibellines in fighting their way home, and broke with them
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/options/3: He swore loyalty to the Scala family
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/explanation: The exiled Whites teamed up with the Ghibellines to fight their way home, and were crushed at La Lastra in 1304. Dante refused to take part and broke with them — a party of one. After that he belonged to no side, and spoke to everyone instead.
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/2/question:
Inferno III, the last line of the writing over the gate of Hell:
“You who enter here, abandon all ___”
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/2/explanation: “Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate” — you who enter here, abandon all hope. Dante cut the deepest despair of his exile into the gate of the Inferno; then he pushed it open, went in, and began to write.
